Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Amina, a 63-year-old auditor, had always prided herself on her meticulous nature and pragmatic view of the world. That changed irrevocably two years ago during what was meant to be a relaxing family picnic at a state park. Her daughter, Layla, had wandered a short distance to admire a patch of wildflowers when a man emerged from the trees, swift and brutal. Amina, frozen by a terror she had never known, watched in horror as Layla was dragged into a dilapidated, locked shed nearby. The memory of Layla’s terrified eyes, her muffled screams, and Amina’s own utter powerlessness to intervene, became the defining moment of her life. The scent of damp earth and pine needles, the rustling of leaves in the breeze, and the metallic clang of the shed door as it locked, were seared into her mind.

In the weeks and months that followed, Amina found her world shrinking. The traumatic event itself felt less like a memory and more like a recurring nightmare that could erupt without warning. A sudden breeze carrying the scent of pine could instantly plunge her back into that moment, and the memory would flood her senses completely. She would see the assailant’s face, hear Layla’s pleas, and feel the rough texture of the ground under her knees as if she were still there, paralyzed. Each time, the terror on recall was as profound and visceral as the original experience, leaving her gasping for breath, heart pounding. She had come to believe that her body was her enemy, constantly reacting as if she were still in danger even when she was safe, betraying her with its uncontrollable panic.

Her professional life, once a source of stability, began to suffer. As an auditor, her work often required her to visit various client sites, sometimes involving small, windowless rooms for document review. Now, being in a locked or confined room, even a perfectly ordinary office, would trigger a wave of intense anxiety. The click of a closing door, the feeling of being enclosed, would bring back the image of Layla trapped in the shed, and Amina would find herself sweating, her breath shallow. She started to avoid going to unfamiliar places altogether, convinced that she could not assess the danger in new environments. This meant turning down lucrative contracts that required travel or visiting new businesses, significantly impacting her income and career prospects. She stayed mostly within a small, familiar radius of her home, her routes predictable and her interactions limited.

The hypervigilance became a constant companion. Amina was superalert, watchful, and on guard even in her own home. Every creak of the floorboards, every distant siren, would send a jolt of alarm through her. This perpetual state of readiness made trouble falling or staying asleep a nightly struggle. She would lie awake for hours, replaying the event, or bolt upright in bed from a nightmare, the terror of victim memories still fresh. What frightened her most was the pervasive feeling of helplessness. She couldn’t stop bad things from happening to her daughter, and she was certain she couldn't stop them from happening again. This conviction led to a profound loss of faith in people, in the inherent goodness of life, and in any higher power that might protect them. The world, she now believed, was an unpredictable and dangerous place where safety was an illusion.

After nearly two years of living in this constant state of dread and isolation, a particularly vivid flashback triggered by a news report about a missing person, combined with the realization that she had not left her neighborhood in weeks, finally prompted Amina to seek help. She felt trapped, not just by the memories, but by the walls of fear she had built around herself, desperately hoping to find a way to reclaim some semblance of the life she had lost.
